passages.title: Buffering of arterial plasma
paragraphs: Arterial plasma is held within roughly 0.04 pH units of 7.40 despite a daily acid load of 50–100 mmol of non-volatile acid. The dominant buffer is the carbon dioxide / bicarbonate pair, whose behaviour is described by pH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PCO₂)), where bicarbonate is in mmol/L and the partial pressure of carbon dioxide is in mmHg. The factor 0.03 converts PCO₂ to the concentration of dissolved CO₂ in mmol/L.

A buffer resists pH change most strongly when the pH of the solution equals the pKa of the buffering pair, because the two forms are then present in equal amounts. The apparent pKa of this pair is 6.1, more than a full unit below the pH it is asked to defend, and in a closed container a buffer this far from its pKa would be a poor one.

What rescues it is that the system is not closed. Dissolved CO₂ is in equilibrium with alveolar gas, and the respiratory centre adjusts ventilation in response to arterial pH and PCO₂ within minutes. Acid added to plasma is converted to CO₂ and breathed off, so the denominator of the ratio is actively held down rather than rising as acid accumulates. The kidney adjusts the numerator over hours to days by reclaiming filtered bicarbonate and excreting ammonium.
Researchers measured arterial blood gases in four patients presenting to an emergency department, shown in Table 1. Reference ranges are pH 7.35–7.45, PCO₂ 35–45 mmHg, and bicarbonate 22–26 mmol/L.

figure.caption: Table 1  Arterial blood gas measurements in four patients.

passages.title: Temperature dependence of a hydrolysis reaction
paragraphs: The rate constant of most reactions varies with temperature according to k = A exp(-Eₐ/RT), where Eₐ is the activation energy, R is 8.314 J/(mol K) and T is the absolute temperature. Taking logarithms gives ln k = ln A - Eₐ/(RT), so a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line whose gradient is -Eₐ/R.

A research group studied the hydrolysis of a phosphate ester that is also a substrate of alkaline phosphatase. The uncatalysed reaction was followed at five temperatures between 288 K and 328 K in buffer at pH 8.0, and the enzyme-catalysed reaction was followed at 310 K. From the uncatalysed data the group reported an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol. With enzyme present the apparent activation energy fell to 25 kJ/mol, while the measured pre-exponential factor was unchanged within error.

A second group repeated the enzyme-catalysed measurement between 310 K and 340 K and found that the rate rose with temperature to a maximum near 320 K and then fell sharply, even though substrate was still in large excess.

passages.title: Flow through a narrowed artery
paragraphs: For steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid cylindrical tube, the volume flow rate is Q = (π r⁴ ΔP) / (8 η L), where r is the radius, ΔP the pressure difference across the length L, and η the viscosity. Because the radius is raised to the fourth power, small changes in calibre have large consequences for flow at a fixed driving pressure.

Where a vessel narrows, the volume passing any cross-section per second must be the same on both sides of the narrowing, so A₁ v₁ = A₂ v₂. Bernoulli's relation then requires that the faster-moving fluid inside the narrowing be at lower pressure: P + (1/2) ρ v² + ρ g h is constant along a streamline for an ideal fluid.

A clinician images a coronary artery and finds a segment where the lumen area has fallen to 40% of the value in the adjacent healthy vessel. Blood velocity in the healthy segment is 0.30 m/s. Take the density of blood as 1060 kg/m³ and treat the vessel as horizontal.

sources.label: NIST, viscosity and density reference data

passages.title: Correcting the optics of the eye
paragraphs: A thin lens obeys 1/f = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ, and its power in dioptres is P = 1/f with f in metres. Lens powers in contact add, so a corrective lens placed in front of the eye adds its power to that of the eye itself. A converging lens has positive power; a diverging lens has negative power.

The unaided eye focuses light from a range of distances between its near point and its far point. In a myopic eye the far point is closer than infinity, so distant objects cannot be brought to a focus on the retina. In presbyopia the near point recedes with age as the lens stiffens, so close work becomes impossible even though distance vision may be unaffected.

A patient is found to have a far point of 40 cm and, at a later visit some years on, a near point of 66.7 cm. A technician in the same clinic assembles a compound microscope from an objective of focal length 4.0 mm and an eyepiece of focal length 25 mm, with the tube length arranged so that the objective forms an image 160 mm beyond its focal point.

passages.title: An amperometric glucose biosensor
paragraphs: A continuous glucose monitor measures current rather than concentration. Glucose oxidase immobilised on an electrode oxidises glucose to gluconolactone, releasing two electrons per molecule. Rather than passing those electrons to O₂, the sensor uses a ferricyanide mediator that is reduced to ferrocyanide at the enzyme and re-oxidised at the working electrode, so the current the instrument reads is proportional to the rate at which glucose is consumed.

The relevant standard reduction potentials at pH 7 are +0.36 V for the ferricyanide / ferrocyanide couple and -0.45 V for the gluconolactone / glucose couple. Standard free energy change and cell potential are related by ΔG = -nFE, with F = 96 485 C/mol. Away from standard conditions the cell potential follows the Nernst equation, which at 25 ° C takes the form E = E - (0.0592/n) log Q.
In a calibration run the instrument integrated the current over a fixed sampling window and recorded a total charge of 9.65 mC.

passages.title: Isolating a carboxylic acid drug
paragraphs: A student is given a crude mixture containing a carboxylic acid drug with a pKa of 4.4, a neutral ester of similar molecular mass, and inorganic salts. The mixture is dissolved in diethyl ether and shaken with aqueous sodium bicarbonate in a separating funnel. The two layers are separated, the aqueous layer is acidified to pH 2 with hydrochloric acid, and a white solid precipitates.

The solid is purified and analysed. Its infrared spectrum shows a very broad absorption spanning roughly 2500 to 3300 wavenumbers together with a strong sharp band at 1710 wavenumbers. Its proton NMR spectrum shows a six-proton doublet, a one-proton multiplet, a two-proton doublet, and a one-proton signal far downfield that disappears when the sample is shaken with D2O.
Purity is checked by thin-layer chromatography on silica with an ether / hexane eluent. The sample spot travels 3.2 cm from the baseline while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm.

passages.title: Calcium oxalate and kidney stones
paragraphs: Most kidney stones are calcium oxalate. The solid dissolves according to CaC2O4(s) in equilibrium with Ca2+(aq) + C2O4 2-(aq), for which the solubility product at 37 ° C is approximately 2.3 × 10⁻⁹. Urine supersaturated in either ion favours crystal growth, which is why prevention targets the concentration of both rather than of the salt as a whole.

Oxalate is the conjugate base of oxalic acid, a diprotic acid whose second ionisation corresponds to a pKa of about 4.3. Urine pH in healthy adults ranges from roughly 4.5 to 8.0 depending on diet and time of day, so the fraction of dissolved oxalate present as the fully deprotonated ion varies substantially across the day. Dietary calcium complicates the picture: calcium eaten with a meal binds oxalate in the gut and reduces how much oxalate is absorbed, so restricting calcium can raise urinary oxalate rather than lower it.

Citrate is prescribed to some stone formers. It chelates calcium in urine, forming a soluble complex that holds calcium in solution and so lowers the free calcium available to the equilibrium above. It also raises urine pH, which has its own consequences for the oxalate equilibrium.
A clinician compares two laboratory samples: one of pure water saturated with calcium oxalate, and one of a 0.010 M calcium chloride solution saturated with the same salt. Both are held at 37 ° C.

passages.title: Forces during walking
paragraphs: A 70 kg adult walks across a force plate that records the vertical ground reaction force. The trace shows two peaks per step: the first as the foot accepts the body's weight, the second as the foot pushes off. Between them is a trough, during which the centre of mass passes over the planted foot and the vertical force dips below body weight. In normal walking the larger peak reaches about 1.2 times body weight. Take g as 9.8 m/s².

The centre of mass rises and falls by about 5 cm over each stride, reaching its highest point at the middle of stance and its lowest at the moment both feet are on the ground. A stride at a comfortable pace takes 0.60 s.

Walking is comparatively efficient because much of the energy lifted into the centre of mass on one half of the stride is recovered on the other, in the way a pendulum exchanges height for speed. The exchange is not perfect: the muscles must supply the shortfall each stride, and the shortfall grows as speed rises. Above roughly 2 m/s the exchange breaks down and most people switch to running, in which the elastic recoil of tendons replaces the pendulum as the energy store.
Running changes the force profile as well. The two peaks merge into a single, larger one, and the ground reaction force at a comfortable running pace reaches two to three times body weight.

passages.title: The thermodynamics of folding
paragraphs: A small globular protein folds reversibly between a folded and an unfolded state with no detectable intermediate, so the transition can be treated as a two-state equilibrium. Calorimetry on the folding transition gives an enthalpy change of -120 kJ/mol and an entropy change of -350 J/(mol K) for the protein itself, and both are roughly constant over the range studied. Spontaneity is set by ΔG = dH - T dS.

The negative entropy term is the cost of ordering a flexible chain into a single structure. An unfolded chain samples an enormous number of conformations; a folded one occupies essentially a single arrangement, and that collapse in accessible states is expensive.

It is paid for by the hydrophobic effect. Non-polar side chains in water force the surrounding molecules into ordered cages, and burying those side chains in the protein's core releases that caged water. The entropy gained is large, but it belongs to the solvent and so is not counted in the -350 J/(mol K) quoted above, which describes the protein alone. Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts within the folded core supply most of the favourable enthalpy.

The protein unfolds when the folded state is no longer favoured. Because the entropy term is multiplied by temperature while the enthalpy term is not, the balance between them shifts as the protein is warmed.

passages.title: The membrane as a circuit
paragraphs: A patch of axonal membrane behaves electrically like a resistor and a capacitor in parallel. The lipid bilayer separates charge and so stores it, giving a membrane capacitance close to 1.0 microfarad per square centimetre in essentially every cell. Ion channels provide a conducting path across it; in a resting unmyelinated axon the membrane resistance is about 1.0 × 10⁴ ohm cm².

When current is injected, the membrane potential does not change instantly. It approaches its new value exponentially with a time constant given by the product of resistance and capacitance, which sets how quickly a synaptic input can change the potential and therefore how briefly two inputs can be separated and still add together.

Myelination wraps many layers of membrane around the axon. Capacitors in series combine so that the total capacitance is lower than any individual one, while the many layers also raise the resistance across the sheath.

questions.stem: Using the relationship in the passage, what is the plasma pH of Patient W?
questions.explanation: The ratio is 24 / (0.03 × 40) = 24 / 1.2 = 20, and log 20 = log 2 + 1 = 1.30. Adding that to the pKa of 6.1 gives 7.40 - the value the passage names as normal, which is the fastest way to confirm the arithmetic without a calculator.

wrong.A: 7.10 is what you get if the ratio is 10 rather than 20, which would require a PCO₂ of 80 mmHg.
wrong.B: 7.26 does not follow from any pairing of the values given; it is roughly what you get by taking log 15, which no part of the calculation produces.
wrong.D: 7.55 overshoots because log 20 is 1.30, not 1.45. Remember log 2 = 0.30, so log 20 = 1.30 exactly.

questions.stem: Patient X is acidotic. What is this patient's plasma pH?
questions.explanation: The ratio is 12 / (0.03 × 24) = 12 / 0.72 = 16.7. Since log 16.7 falls between log 10 and log 20, the pH must fall between 7.10 and 7.40, which already eliminates two choices. Taking log 16.7 as about 1.22 gives 6.1 + 1.22 = 7.32.

wrong.A: 7.12 uses the normal PCO₂ of 40 mmHg rather than this patient's 24 mmHg, which gives a ratio of 10 instead of 16.7.
wrong.B: 7.22 would need a ratio of about 13, which means dividing 12 by 0.9 rather than by 0.72.
wrong.D: 7.42 is above normal, but this patient has lost proportionally more bicarbonate than CO₂, so the ratio and the pH must both fall.

questions.stem: Which patient's values are most consistent with a primary respiratory problem that the kidney has had time to compensate for?

choices.D: Patient Z

questions.explanation: Patient Y has a raised PCO₂ (60 mmHg), which is a respiratory disturbance because PCO₂ is set by ventilation, together with a bicarbonate above range (26 mmol/L). Renal compensation is the slow arm of the system described in the passage, so a bicarbonate that has risen to defend the ratio points to a respiratory problem of some standing.

wrong.A: Patient W has entirely normal values and so has no disturbance to compensate for.
wrong.B: Patient X has a low bicarbonate with a low PCO₂, which is a metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation - the reverse of what is asked.
wrong.D: Patient Z has a high bicarbonate with a low PCO₂. The primary problem is the metabolic alkalosis; a kidney compensating for a respiratory problem would not drive bicarbonate to 36 mmol/L.

questions.stem: If a patient's PCO₂ rose from 40 to 80 mmHg while bicarbonate stayed at 24 mmol/L, the plasma pH would:

choices.D: be unchanged, because bicarbonate did not change

questions.explanation: Doubling PCO₂ halves the ratio, and the logarithm of a halved quantity is 0.30 lower, so the pH falls from 7.40 to 7.10. This is worth recognising on sight: every doubling of PCO₂ at fixed bicarbonate costs 0.30 pH units.

wrong.B: 0.60 units would be two doublings - a PCO₂ of 160 mmHg.
wrong.C: The direction is wrong. CO₂ is the acid member of the pair, so more of it lowers the pH.
wrong.D: The pH depends on the ratio of the two, not on bicarbonate alone, so a change in either moves it.

questions.stem: The passage argues that a buffer is most effective when the solution pH equals the buffer pKa, yet the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ pair buffers plasma well at pH 7.40. The best explanation is that:

choices.A: ventilation removes the acid member of the pair, so its concentration does not rise as acid is added
choices.B: the apparent pKa of the pair rises to 7.4 at body temperature
choices.C: bicarbonate is present at a far higher concentration than any other plasma buffer
choices.D: plasma proteins and phosphate buffer the pH instead, leaving the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ pair unused

questions.explanation: The passage makes exactly this point: the system is open, and the respiratory centre holds the CO₂ term down rather than letting it climb. Closed-system buffer reasoning, which is where the pKa rule comes from, does not apply when one member is continuously vented.

wrong.B: The passage gives the apparent pKa as 6.1 and does not describe it shifting with temperature; invoking an unstated shift is unnecessary once the open system is recognised.
wrong.C: Bicarbonate's concentration contributes to buffer capacity, but a high concentration of a buffer far from its pKa still buffers poorly. Concentration alone does not resolve the paradox the passage raises.
wrong.D: Both do contribute, but the passage identifies the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ pair as dominant, so an explanation that sidelines it contradicts the text.

questions.stem: What does the gradient of a plot of ln k against 1/T give for the uncatalysed reaction?

choices.A: -Eₐ/R, so a gradient of about -4.2 × 10² K
choices.B: +Eₐ/R, so a gradient of about +6.0 × 10³ K
choices.C: ln A, which is independent of temperature
choices.D: -Eₐ/R, so a gradient of about -6.0 × 10³ K

questions.explanation: The passage gives the gradient as -Eₐ/R. With Eₐ = 50 000 J/mol and R = 8.314 J/(mol K), Eₐ/R = 6.0 × 10³ K, so the gradient is -6.0 × 10³ K. The sign is negative because the rate rises as 1/T falls.

wrong.A: 4.2 × 10² K comes from dividing 50 000 by 120 or similar; dividing by 8.314 gives roughly 6000, not 420.
wrong.B: The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong. Rearranged, ln k = ln A - Eₐ/(RT), so the coefficient of 1/T carries a minus sign.
wrong.C: ln A is the intercept of this plot, not its gradient.

questions.stem: By approximately what factor does the uncatalysed rate constant increase on warming from 298 K to 310 K?
questions.explanation: The ratio is exp[-(Eₐ/R)(1/310–1/298)]. The bracket is about -1.30 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, and multiplying by Eₐ/R = 6.0 × 10³ K gives an exponent of about +0.78, so the ratio is e⁰.78, roughly 2.2. The familiar rule of thumb that rates roughly double over a 10 degree rise is doing the same arithmetic.

wrong.A: 1.04 is the ratio of the temperatures themselves, 310/298. Rate depends exponentially on 1/T, not linearly on T.
wrong.B: 12 would require an activation energy several times larger than 50 kJ/mol over this interval.
wrong.C: Raising the temperature increases the fraction of collisions carrying at least Eₐ, so the rate constant of an uncatalysed step rises.

questions.stem: Taking the pre-exponential factor as unchanged, by roughly what factor does the enzyme raise the rate at 310 K?
questions.explanation: With A unchanged, the ratio of rate constants is exp[(50 000–25 000)/(R x 310)] = exp(25 000/2577) = exp(9.7), which is about 1.6 × 10⁴. Halving the activation energy does far more than halve the barrier's cost, because it sits in an exponent.

wrong.A: A factor of 2 would follow if rate were proportional to 1/Eₐ. It is not; Eₐ appears in an exponent.
wrong.B: 10² corresponds to an exponent near 4.6, which would need the activation energy to fall by only about 12 kJ/mol.
wrong.D: 10⁶ needs an exponent near 13.8, which would require a drop of about 36 kJ/mol rather than 25.

questions.stem: What best explains the second group's finding that the catalysed rate falls above about 320 K?

choices.A: The activation energy of the catalysed reaction rises with temperature
choices.B: The reaction becomes endothermic above 320 K
choices.C: Substrate becomes limiting at higher temperature
choices.D: The enzyme denatures, so the concentration of functional catalyst falls

questions.explanation: Arrhenius behaviour predicts a monotonic rise, so a fall means the catalyst itself is being lost. Above a protein's melting range the tertiary structure unfolds and the active site is destroyed, and that loss outruns the Arrhenius gain.

wrong.A: Activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway, and treating it as temperature-dependent here invents a mechanism when a much simpler one fits.
wrong.B: Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic is a thermodynamic property that does not flip at a particular temperature, and in any case it sets the position of equilibrium rather than the rate.
wrong.C: The passage states that substrate was still in large excess, so saturation cannot explain the fall.

questions.stem: Independently of the case described, if disease narrowed a vessel's radius by 20% at a fixed pressure difference, flow through it would fall to approximately:

choices.D: 41% of its original value

questions.explanation: Flow goes as r⁴, so the fraction remaining is 0.8⁴ = 0.41, or 41%. This is the single most useful consequence of Poiseuille's relation: a fifth off the radius costs nearly 60% of the flow.

wrong.A: 20% confuses the fraction taken off the radius with the fraction of flow left behind.
wrong.B: 64% is 0.8³, which would be the answer if flow went as the cube of the radius.
wrong.C: 80% treats flow as proportional to radius. The fourth power is the whole point of the relation.

questions.stem: What is the blood velocity inside the narrowed segment?
questions.explanation: Continuity applies to area, and the passage gives the area as 40% of healthy. So v₂ = v₁ x (A₁/A₂) = 0.30 × (1/0.40) = 0.75 m/s. Note that the area ratio is used once: squaring it would be appropriate only if the passage had given a radius ratio.

wrong.A: 0.12 m/s multiplies by 0.40 instead of dividing by it, which would have fluid slowing as the vessel narrows - impossible if the same volume passes each second.
wrong.B: 0.30 m/s is the velocity in the healthy segment, unchanged. Continuity requires that it rise where the area falls.
wrong.D: 1.9 m/s squares the area ratio. Squaring converts a radius ratio into an area ratio, but the passage has already given the area.

questions.stem: Approximately how much lower is the pressure inside the narrowed segment than in the healthy vessel?
questions.explanation: For a horizontal vessel Bernoulli gives ΔP = (1/2) ρ (v₂² - v₁². With v₁ = 0.30 m/s and v₂ = 0.75 m/s, that is 0.5 × 1060 × (0.5625–0.09) = 2.5 × 10² Pa, which is under 2 mmHg - small, because these velocities are low.

wrong.A: 48 Pa is the dynamic pressure of the healthy segment alone, 0.5 × 1060 × 0.30². It leaves out the faster fluid inside the narrowing, which is where the pressure actually falls.
wrong.C: 1.8 × 10³ Pa follows from taking the velocity in the narrowing as 1.9 m/s, which comes from squaring an area ratio the passage had already given as an area.
wrong.D: 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa is roughly two atmospheres. A sanity check against arterial pressures, which span about 1.3 × 10⁴ Pa, rules it out immediately.

questions.stem: The passage's flow relation assumes a rigid tube. A real artery is elastic, and the pressure inside the narrowed segment is lower than outside it. Compared with the rigid-tube prediction, flow through the diseased segment should therefore be:

choices.A: lower, because the drop in internal pressure tends to collapse the segment further
choices.B: higher, because an elastic wall stores energy and returns it to the fluid
choices.C: identical, because Bernoulli's relation already accounts for wall elasticity
choices.D: higher, because elastic walls reduce the effective viscosity of blood

questions.explanation: Bernoulli requires lower pressure where the fluid moves faster, and a compliant wall responds to a lower internal pressure by narrowing further. That reduces the radius, which by the fourth-power relation reduces flow below the rigid-tube prediction - a self-reinforcing effect that matters clinically.

wrong.B: Elastic storage redistributes energy over the cardiac cycle but does not add energy, and the question asks about the steady narrowing rather than pulsatile recoil.
wrong.C: Bernoulli's relation is written for an ideal fluid in a fixed geometry and says nothing about how the wall responds.
wrong.D: Viscosity is a property of the blood, not of the wall.

questions.stem: What power of corrective lens does the patient need to see distant objects clearly?
questions.explanation: The lens must take light from infinity and make it appear to come from the far point, 40 cm in front of the eye, which means a virtual image at -0.40 m. Then P = 1/(-0.40) = -2.5 D. The negative sign is the useful check: myopia is always corrected with a diverging lens.

wrong.B: -0.4 D inverts the arithmetic, using 0.40 m directly rather than its reciprocal.
wrong.C: +0.4 D has both the magnitude and the sign wrong.
wrong.D: +2.5 D has the right magnitude but a converging lens would move the far point closer still, making distance vision worse.

questions.stem: At the later visit, what additional power is needed to let the patient read at 25 cm?
questions.explanation: The reading lens must take an object at 25 cm and form an image at the near point, 66.7 cm, so P = 1/0.25–1/0.667 = 4.0–1.5 = +2.5 D. Working in dioptres rather than centimetres keeps this to one subtraction.

wrong.A: +1.5 D is the 1/0.667 term on its own, which is the power the eye can already manage.
wrong.C: +4.0 D is the 1/0.25 term on its own and ignores what the eye still does unaided.
wrong.D: +5.5 D adds the two terms instead of subtracting, which would overcorrect substantially.

questions.stem: The image the objective of the microscope forms is best described as:

choices.D: virtual and upright

questions.explanation: The objective is a converging lens with the specimen just outside its focal length, so it forms a real, inverted image inside the tube. That real image then serves as the object for the eyepiece, which magnifies it as a virtual image.

wrong.B: A single converging lens forming a real image always inverts it.
wrong.C: The image is formed inside the tube where it can act as a real object for the eyepiece, so it is real rather than virtual.
wrong.D: Virtual and upright describes what the eyepiece produces, not the objective.

questions.stem: Taking the near point of the relaxed eye as 25 cm, the approximate total magnification of the microscope is:
questions.explanation: The objective contributes image distance over focal length, 160 / 4.0 = 40x. The eyepiece acts as a magnifier contributing 250 / 25 = 10x with both lengths in millimetres. Multiplying gives about 400x.

wrong.A: 40x is the objective's contribution alone, and ignores the eyepiece.
wrong.B: 100x would need an eyepiece contributing 2.5x rather than the 10x its 25 mm focal length gives.
wrong.D: 4000x is a factor-of-ten slip, most often from mixing millimetres and centimetres in the eyepiece term.

questions.stem: What is the standard cell potential of this sensor?
questions.explanation: Cell potential is the cathode's reduction potential minus the anode's. Ferricyanide is reduced at the electrode and glucose is oxidised, so E = 0.36 - (-0.45) = 0.81 V. Subtracting a negative number is where most slips happen here.

wrong.A: 0.09 V adds the two values instead of subtracting, which drops the sign on the glucose couple.
wrong.B: 0.45 V is the glucose couple alone with its sign flipped, and ignores the mediator entirely.
wrong.D: 1.26 V adds 0.36 to 0.90, doubling the glucose term.

questions.stem: What is the standard free energy change for the reaction as written, per mole of glucose?

choices.D: -313 kJ/mol

questions.explanation: ΔG = -nFE with n = 2 and E = 0.81 V gives -(2)(96 485)(0.81) = -1.56 × 10⁵ J/mol, or -156 kJ/mol. A positive cell potential must give a negative ΔG, which is the sign check worth doing before the arithmetic.

wrong.A: The sign is wrong. A spontaneous cell has a positive potential and therefore a negative free energy change.
wrong.B: -78 kJ/mol uses n = 1. The passage states that two electrons are released per glucose.
wrong.D: -313 kJ/mol uses n = 4, which would be two glucose molecules rather than one.

questions.stem: At which electrode does glucose react, and what is that electrode called?

choices.A: The working electrode; it is the cathode
choices.B: The working electrode; it is the anode
choices.C: The enzyme layer; it is the cathode
choices.D: The enzyme layer; it is the anode

questions.explanation: Oxidation defines the anode, and glucose is oxidised at the immobilised enzyme layer. The electrons then travel via the mediator to the working electrode, where ferricyanide is reduced - that electrode is the cathode.

wrong.A: Glucose does not react at the working electrode; the mediator does. And oxidation never happens at a cathode.
wrong.B: The electrode is correctly named an anode here, but the passage places the glucose reaction at the enzyme, not at the working electrode.
wrong.C: The site is right but the name is wrong: oxidation happens at an anode, by definition.

questions.stem: If the ratio of ferrocyanide to ferricyanide at the working electrode rose by a factor of ten, the cell potential would fall by approximately:
questions.explanation: A tenfold change in Q changes log Q by exactly 1, so the Nernst term changes by 0.0592/n. With n = 2 that is 0.0296 V, about 0.030 V. Recognising that one factor of ten costs 0.0592/n volts saves the whole calculation.

wrong.A: 0.015 V uses n = 4, which would be four electrons per glucose. The passage gives two, and n sits in the denominator, so halving it doubles the shift rather than halving it.
wrong.C: 0.059 V is the n = 1 value. This cell passes two electrons.
wrong.D: 0.118 V doubles the n = 1 value rather than halving it; n appears in the denominator.

questions.stem: How many moles of glucose were consumed during the calibration window?
questions.explanation: Charge divided by Faraday's constant gives moles of electrons: 9.65 × 10⁻³ / 96 485 = 1.00 × 10⁻⁷ mol. Each glucose releases two electrons, so the glucose consumed is half that, 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ mol.

wrong.A: 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ mol divides by four rather than by two.
wrong.C: 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol is the moles of electrons, not of glucose. The last step is the one being tested.
wrong.D: 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol multiplies by two instead of dividing, which would be right only if two electrons made two glucose.

questions.stem: After the first extraction, where is the drug, and why?

choices.A: In the ether layer, because carboxylic acids are more soluble in organic solvents
choices.B: In the aqueous layer, because bicarbonate protonates it to a charged species
choices.C: Distributed evenly, because its pKa is close to the pH of bicarbonate solution
choices.D: In the aqueous layer, because bicarbonate deprotonates it to a charged carboxylate

questions.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate solution sits near pH 8, well above the drug's pKa of 4.4, so the acid is almost entirely deprotonated. The resulting carboxylate carries a charge and partitions into the water. Acidifying afterwards reprotonates it, which is why the solid then precipitates.

wrong.A: The neutral acid would favour ether, but bicarbonate converts it to its charged conjugate base first.
wrong.B: Bicarbonate is a base in this reaction; it removes a proton rather than adding one.
wrong.C: PH 8 is more than three units above the pKa, so the ratio of base to acid is over a thousand to one - not an even split.

questions.stem: The very broad absorption from 2500 to 3300 wavenumbers is best assigned to:

choices.A: the O-H stretch of a carboxylic acid
choices.B: the N-H stretch of a primary amine
choices.C: the C-H stretch of an aromatic ring
choices.D: the C=O stretch of an ester

questions.explanation: A carboxylic acid O-H gives an unusually broad band over roughly this range because of strong hydrogen-bonded dimers, and it appears alongside the carbonyl band at 1710. Together those two features are close to diagnostic.

wrong.B: A primary amine gives two comparatively sharp bands near 3300, not a band hundreds of wavenumbers wide.
wrong.C: Aromatic C-H stretches are sharp and sit just above 3000.
wrong.D: A C=O stretch is the sharp band at 1710, a different feature of the same spectrum.

questions.stem: What is the retention factor of the sample on the TLC plate?
questions.explanation: Retention factor is the distance travelled by the spot divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front: 3.2 / 8.0 = 0.40. It cannot exceed 1, since the spot cannot outrun the solvent carrying it.

wrong.A: 0.25 inverts part of the ratio or misreads which distance is which.
wrong.B: 0.32 divides the spot distance by 10 cm rather than by the 8.0 cm the solvent front actually travelled.
wrong.D: 2.5 divides the solvent front by the spot. A retention factor above 1 is impossible, since the spot cannot outrun the solvent carrying it.

questions.stem: The one-proton signal that disappears on shaking with D2O is:

choices.D: an aromatic proton

questions.explanation: Protons on oxygen exchange rapidly with deuterium from D2O, so the signal vanishes. The acid proton is the only exchangeable one here, and it is also the furthest downfield, which matches the description.

wrong.A: A methine proton is bound to carbon and does not exchange.
wrong.C: Methyl protons are bound to carbon, do not exchange, and would integrate for six rather than one.
wrong.D: Aromatic protons are bound to carbon and do not exchange.

questions.stem: The six-proton doublet is most consistent with:

choices.A: a single methyl group adjacent to a methylene
choices.C: two methyl groups on a quaternary carbon
choices.D: two equivalent methyl groups on a carbon bearing one hydrogen

questions.explanation: Six equivalent protons means two equivalent methyl groups. Their appearance as a doublet means exactly one neighbouring proton, so those methyls sit on a carbon that itself bears a single hydrogen - an isopropyl group, which also accounts for the one-proton multiplet.

wrong.A: A single methyl integrates for three, not six, and would appear as a triplet next to a methylene.
wrong.B: Three methylene groups would integrate for six but would not appear as a clean doublet, and there is no such arrangement in a molecule this small.
wrong.C: Methyls on a quaternary carbon have no neighbouring protons, so they would be a singlet.

questions.stem: What is the molar solubility of calcium oxalate in pure water at this temperature?
questions.explanation: For a 1:1 salt, Ksp = s², so s is the square root of 2.3 × 10⁻⁹. Since the square root of 23 × 10⁻¹⁰ is about 4.8 × 10⁻⁵, that is the molar solubility.

wrong.A: 2.3 × 10⁻⁹ M is the solubility product itself, not the solubility. They have different units and different meanings.
wrong.C: 1.5 × 10⁻³ M is roughly the cube root rather than the square root, which would suit a salt releasing three ions.
wrong.D: 4.8 × 10⁻³ M is off by two orders of magnitude, which comes from halving the exponent of 2.3 × 10⁻⁹ without care.

questions.stem: What is the molar solubility of calcium oxalate in the 0.010 M calcium chloride solution?
questions.explanation: Calcium is already present at 0.010 M, which swamps the small amount the salt contributes. So Ksp = (0.010)(s) and s = 2.3 × 10⁻⁹ / 0.010 = 2.3 × 10⁻⁷ M. The common ion has cut solubility by more than two hundredfold.

wrong.A: 2.3 × 10⁻¹¹ M multiplies by 0.010 rather than dividing, which would make the salt less soluble still.
wrong.C: 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ M divides by 10⁻⁴ rather than by 10⁻².
wrong.D: 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ M is the pure-water value and ignores the common ion entirely.

questions.stem: A patient's urine pH falls from 7.0 to 4.5. The effect on calcium oxalate solubility is to:

choices.A: increase it, because protonation of oxalate lowers the free oxalate concentration
choices.B: increase it, because calcium is displaced by protons from the crystal lattice
choices.C: decrease it, because the solubility product falls as pH falls
choices.D: leave it unchanged, because the solubility product does not depend on pH

questions.explanation: At pH 4.5 a substantial fraction of oxalate is protonated to hydrogen oxalate, since the relevant pKa is 4.3. Removing free oxalate from solution pulls the dissolution equilibrium to the right, so more solid dissolves.

wrong.B: Protons do not exchange for calcium in the lattice; the pH effect acts on the oxalate ion in solution.
wrong.C: A solubility product is an equilibrium constant and does not change with pH; only the concentrations do.
wrong.D: The constant is indeed fixed, but the free oxalate concentration is not, and that is what shifts the equilibrium.

questions.stem: The solubility product of calcium oxalate is best described as:

choices.A: the rate at which the solid dissolves
choices.B: the concentration of solid in equilibrium with its ions
choices.C: the mass of salt that dissolves in one litre
choices.D: the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of the solid

questions.explanation: A solubility product is an equilibrium constant written for the dissolution reaction, so it is the product of the dissolved ion concentrations at equilibrium. The solid itself does not appear, which is why its amount never enters the expression.

wrong.A: Equilibrium constants say nothing about rate. A salt with a tiny Ksp can dissolve quickly up to its limit.
wrong.B: A pure solid has no meaningful concentration term and is omitted from the expression.
wrong.C: That describes solubility in grams per litre, which depends on molar mass as well.

questions.stem: What is the adult's weight?
questions.explanation: Weight is mass times gravitational field strength: 70 × 9.8 = 686 N. Mass in kilograms and weight in newtons are different quantities, and the factor between them here is about ten.

wrong.A: 7.1 N divides by g instead of multiplying by it.
wrong.B: 70 N is the mass in kilograms with the wrong unit attached. Mass and weight are different quantities.
wrong.D: 6860 N uses g = 98 m/s², a factor of ten too large.

questions.stem: What is the approximate magnitude of the larger ground reaction force peak?
questions.explanation: The passage gives the peak as 1.2 times body weight, so 1.2 × 686 = 823 N. The useful idea is that walking is not static: the ground must push harder than body weight to decelerate a falling centre of mass.

wrong.A: 84 N is 1.2 times the mass in kilograms, which is not a force.
wrong.B: 686 N is body weight itself, which is what the force would be only if the person stood still.
wrong.D: 1370 N is twice body weight, which is nearer a running peak than a walking one.

questions.stem: How much work is done against gravity raising the centre of mass during one stride?
questions.explanation: Work against gravity is mgh: 70 × 9.8 × 0.05 = 34.3 J. The commonest error is leaving the height in centimetres, which inflates the answer a hundredfold.

wrong.A: 3.4 J is a factor of ten low, usually from using 0.005 m for the height.
wrong.B: 17 J halves the height, which would be right only if the 5 cm were the full peak-to-peak range and the lift were half of it. The passage gives the rise itself.
wrong.D: 343 J uses h = 0.5 m rather than 0.05 m.

questions.stem: What average power is required for that lifting, over a single stride?
questions.explanation: Power is work over time: 34.3 J in 0.60 s is about 57 W. Dividing by a number less than one must increase the value, which rules out the smaller choice immediately.

wrong.A: 21 W multiplies by 0.60 instead of dividing by it.
wrong.C: 206 W divides the work by 0.166 s, which would be a stride rate of six per second.
wrong.D: 572 W compounds a unit slip in the work term with the division.

questions.stem: The passage compares walking to a pendulum. The point of the comparison is that:

choices.A: the leg swings at its natural frequency, so no muscular work is needed at all
choices.B: the centre of mass moves in a straight line, minimising work
choices.C: the ground reaction force stays equal to body weight throughout
choices.D: gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy are exchanged, so less energy must be supplied each stride

questions.explanation: A pendulum trades height for speed and back again, and the passage says walking recovers much of the energy lifted into the centre of mass. That exchange is why the metabolic cost of walking is far below the work that would be needed to lift and lower the body from scratch each step.

wrong.A: Some recovery does not mean complete recovery; muscles still do work every stride, which is why walking is tiring.
wrong.B: The passage states the centre of mass rises and falls by about 5 cm, so it does not travel in a straight line.
wrong.C: The passage gives a peak of 1.2 times body weight, so the force plainly varies.

questions.stem: What is ΔG for folding at body temperature, 310 K?

choices.D: -120 kJ/mol

questions.explanation: ΔG = dH - T dS = -120 000 - (310)(-350) = -120 000 + 108 500 = -11 500 J/mol, so -11.5 kJ/mol. Note that the entropy term must be converted from joules to match, and that subtracting a negative adds.

wrong.A: +228 kJ/mol adds the two magnitudes, which drops the sign on the enthalpy term.
wrong.B: The sign is wrong, which usually comes from subtracting 108 500 rather than adding it. Subtracting a negative adds.
wrong.D: -120 kJ/mol is the enthalpy alone and ignores the entropy term entirely.

questions.stem: Above approximately what temperature does the protein unfold?
questions.explanation: Unfolding begins where ΔG for folding reaches zero, so T = dH / dS = 120 000 / 350 = 343 K, about 70 ° C. Above that the unfavourable entropy term outweighs the favourable enthalpy term and the folded state is no longer stable.

wrong.A: 298 K is standard room temperature and has nothing to do with this protein's numbers.
wrong.B: 310 K is body temperature, where the previous calculation shows the free energy change is still negative and the protein is folded.
wrong.D: 373 K is the boiling point of water, not a value derived from the enthalpy and entropy given.

questions.stem: The entropy change for the protein itself is negative because:

choices.A: a folded chain has far fewer accessible conformations than an unfolded one
choices.B: heat is released as the protein folds
choices.C: water molecules become more ordered around the folded protein
choices.D: the folded state has lower energy

questions.explanation: Entropy counts accessible microstates. An unfolded chain can adopt an enormous number of conformations and a folded one essentially adopts a single structure, so folding reduces the protein's own entropy sharply.

wrong.B: Released heat is the enthalpy term, which is a separate quantity.
wrong.C: The passage says the opposite: ordered water is released on burying hydrophobic side chains, and in any case that entropy is counted in the solvent.
wrong.D: Lower energy describes enthalpy, not entropy. The two are independent in this expression.

questions.stem: A mutation makes folding more exothermic without changing the entropy of folding. Compared with the original protein, the mutant will:

choices.B: unfold at the same temperature, because dS is unchanged
choices.D: unfold at a higher temperature

questions.explanation: The unfolding temperature is dH / dS. Making dH more negative increases the magnitude of that ratio, so the temperature at which the entropy term finally wins is higher. A more exothermic folding reaction buys thermal stability.

wrong.A: That would follow from a smaller enthalpy magnitude, not a larger one.
wrong.B: The temperature depends on both terms, so changing either moves it.
wrong.C: A more favourable enthalpy makes folding more spontaneous, not less.

questions.stem: What is the membrane time constant for this patch?

choices.D: 100 ms

questions.explanation: The time constant is the product of resistance and capacitance: (1.0 × 10⁴ ohm cm²(1.0 × 10⁻⁶ F/cm² = 1.0 × 10⁻² s, which is 10 ms. The area units cancel, which is the clue that the two quantities are meant to be multiplied as given.

wrong.A: 1.0 × 10⁻² ms is the answer in seconds mislabelled as milliseconds, a factor of a thousand out.
wrong.B: 1.0 ms would need either a tenfold smaller resistance or a tenfold smaller capacitance.
wrong.D: 100 ms is ten times too large, usually from taking the capacitance as 10 microfarads.

questions.stem: Compared with an unmyelinated axon, a myelinated one has a membrane time constant that is:

choices.A: shorter, because both capacitance and resistance fall
choices.B: longer, because resistance rises and capacitance is unchanged
choices.C: unchanged, because resistance and capacitance change by the same factor
choices.D: shorter, because capacitance falls more than resistance rises

questions.explanation: Myelin cuts capacitance sharply, since capacitors in series give a total smaller than any one of them, while resistance rises. The net effect in real axons is a shorter time constant and faster conduction, which is the point of myelin.

wrong.A: The passage states that the many layers raise resistance; they do not lower it.
wrong.B: Capacitance is not unchanged - the passage makes the series combination explicit.
wrong.C: If the two changed by the same factor in the same direction the product would move, not stay put; and here they move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Three identical resistors are connected in parallel. The resistance of the combination is:

choices.A: three times that of one resistor
choices.B: one third that of one resistor
choices.C: equal to that of one resistor
choices.D: the square root of that of one resistor

questions.explanation: Parallel paths add conductance, so n identical resistors in parallel give R/n. Physically, opening more channels across a membrane gives current more routes and so lowers resistance - which is exactly what channel opening does.

wrong.A: Three times is the series result.
wrong.C: Adding a parallel path always lowers resistance below that of the single path.
wrong.D: No combination rule produces a square root.

questions.stem: Two synaptic inputs arriving 5 ms apart sum more effectively in this unmyelinated patch than two arriving 50 ms apart because:

choices.A: the second input arrives before the first has decayed appreciably
choices.B: the membrane resistance falls between the two arriving inputs
choices.C: the capacitance of the membrane rises with stimulation frequency
choices.D: an input arriving sooner produces a larger postsynaptic potential

questions.explanation: With a time constant of 10 ms, 5 ms is half a time constant and the first input has lost only a fraction of its effect, so the two potentials add. After 50 ms, five time constants have passed and almost nothing of the first remains. This is temporal summation, and the membrane time constant sets its window.

wrong.B: Nothing in the passage changes resistance between inputs, and a fall in resistance would shorten the summation window rather than widen it.
wrong.C: Membrane capacitance is fixed by the bilayer at about 1 μF/cm² and does not vary with how often the cell is stimulated.
wrong.D: The size of a postsynaptic potential is set by the synapse, not by when the input happens to arrive.

questions.stem: Which compound has the highest boiling point?

choices.D: CH3CH2CH2CH3

questions.explanation: Ethanol is the only one of these that can donate a hydrogen bond, since its hydrogen sits on oxygen. Hydrogen bonding is far stronger than the dispersion forces available to the others, so ethanol boils well above them despite its modest mass.

wrong.A: Propane has only dispersion forces and the lowest mass here, so it boils lowest of all.
wrong.C: Dimethyl ether can accept a hydrogen bond but has no O-H to donate, so ether molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
wrong.D: Butane is heavier than ethanol and so has stronger dispersion forces, but dispersion alone does not match hydrogen bonding at this size.

questions.stem: Ice floats on liquid water because:

choices.A: hydrogen bonding holds the molecules in an open lattice with more space between them
choices.B: hydrogen bonds in ice are weaker than in liquid water
choices.C: ice contains trapped air that lowers its density
choices.D: water molecules in ice are smaller than in the liquid

questions.explanation: Each water molecule in ice is hydrogen bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement, and that geometry holds the molecules further apart on average than the jostling of the liquid does. More space per molecule means lower density, so ice floats.

wrong.B: Hydrogen bonds in ice are stronger and more ordered, not weaker. That is precisely why the lattice is rigid.
wrong.C: Pure ice frozen from degassed water still floats, so trapped air cannot be the explanation.
wrong.D: A molecule's size does not change on freezing; only the spacing between molecules does.

questions.stem: Which molecule is non-polar despite containing polar bonds?

choices.D: CO₂

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is linear, so its two C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel exactly. Polarity depends on geometry as much as on electronegativity: symmetric arrangements cancel, bent or pyramidal ones do not.

wrong.A: Water is bent, so its two O-H dipoles add to a substantial net dipole rather than cancelling.
wrong.B: Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, and its lone pair makes the arrangement asymmetric.
wrong.C: Chloroform is tetrahedral with three chlorines and one hydrogen, which is not symmetric enough to cancel.

questions.stem: At pH 7.0, glycine (pKa values 2.3 and 9.6) exists predominantly as:

choices.A: a cation with a protonated amine and a protonated carboxyl
choices.B: a zwitterion with a deprotonated carboxyl and a protonated amine
choices.C: an anion with a deprotonated carboxyl and a neutral amine
choices.D: a neutral molecule with a protonated carboxyl and a neutral amine

questions.explanation: At pH 7.0 the solution sits well above the carboxyl pKa of 2.3, so that group is deprotonated, and well below the amino pKa of 9.6, so that group is still protonated. The result carries both a negative and a positive charge with no net charge: the zwitterion.

wrong.A: A protonated carboxyl would need a pH below 2.3, more than four units lower than this.
wrong.C: A neutral amine would need a pH above 9.6. At pH 7.0 the amine is still holding its proton.
wrong.D: This combination requires a pH both below 2.3 and above 9.6 at once, which is impossible.

questions.stem: The peptide bond shows restricted rotation because:

choices.A: the carbonyl oxygen hydrogen bonds to the amide hydrogen
choices.B: delocalisation gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character
choices.C: the adjacent side chains are too bulky to allow rotation
choices.D: the nitrogen is sp3 hybridised and therefore rigid

questions.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the carbonyl, so the C-N bond carries partial double-bond character. Double bonds do not rotate freely, which is why the peptide unit is planar and why proteins have a limited set of backbone conformations.

wrong.A: That hydrogen bond forms between different residues in secondary structure and does not fix rotation about the bond itself.
wrong.C: Glycine has only a hydrogen for a side chain and its peptide bonds are just as restricted, so bulk is not the cause.
wrong.D: Delocalisation makes the nitrogen effectively sp2, and sp3 hybridisation would permit rotation rather than prevent it.

questions.stem: A student has a sample of a chiral drug and wants to establish whether it is a single enantiomer or a racemic mixture. The most direct measurement is:

choices.A: optical rotation in a polarimeter, since a racemate rotates plane-polarised light not at all
choices.B: melting point, since enantiomers melt at different temperatures
choices.C: infrared spectroscopy, since enantiomers absorb at different wavenumbers
choices.D: mass spectrometry, since enantiomers differ in molecular mass

questions.explanation: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions, so an equal mixture gives zero net rotation while a single enantiomer gives a measurable one. That difference is the defining physical distinction between them.

wrong.B: Enantiomers have identical melting points. A racemate can melt differently from the pure enantiomer, but that comparison needs a pure reference the student does not have.
wrong.C: Enantiomers have identical infrared spectra, because the bonds and their force constants are the same.
wrong.D: Enantiomers have identical molecular masses, since they contain exactly the same atoms.

questions.stem: A substitution on a tertiary alkyl halide in a polar protic solvent proceeds with racemisation. This is most consistent with:

choices.A: an SN2 mechanism, because the nucleophile attacks from the back
choices.B: an SN1 mechanism, because a planar carbocation can be attacked from either face
choices.C: an E1 mechanism, because elimination destroys the stereocentre
choices.D: an SN2 mechanism, because the solvent stabilises the transition state

questions.explanation: A tertiary centre in a protic solvent favours ionisation to a carbocation, which is trigonal planar. A nucleophile can then attack either face with roughly equal probability, giving both configurations. Racemisation is the signature of a planar intermediate.

wrong.A: Back-side attack inverts configuration cleanly rather than racemising it, and a tertiary centre is too hindered for SN2 anyway.
wrong.C: Elimination produces an alkene, not a substitution product, so it cannot be the pathway for the product described.
wrong.D: The solvent description is accurate but the mechanism is not: protic solvents stabilise carbocations and hinder SN2 by caging the nucleophile.

questions.stem: In size-exclusion chromatography, the first proteins to elute are:

choices.A: the largest, because they cannot enter the pores of the beads
choices.B: the smallest, because they travel through the column fastest
choices.C: the most positively charged, because they are repelled by the resin
choices.D: the most hydrophobic, because they interact least with water

questions.explanation: Large proteins are excluded from the pores and so travel only through the space between beads, which is the shorter path. Small proteins enter the pores, take a longer route, and elute later. The separation is by size alone, with no binding involved.

wrong.B: Small proteins enter the pores, which lengthens their path, so they elute last rather than first.
wrong.C: Charge-based separation is ion exchange, a different technique.
wrong.D: Hydrophobic interaction is another technique entirely, and size exclusion is designed to avoid binding of any kind.

questions.stem: A researcher separates proteins by SDS-PAGE and finds a single band. To test whether the sample is genuinely one protein rather than two of equal mass, the most informative additional experiment is:

choices.A: repeating the gel with a longer run time
choices.B: running the sample on an isoelectric focusing gel, which separates by charge rather than mass
choices.C: increasing the SDS concentration to ensure complete denaturation
choices.D: staining the gel with a more sensitive dye

questions.explanation: Two proteins of the same mass are indistinguishable by a method that separates on mass alone, however carefully it is run. Isoelectric focusing separates by isoelectric point, so it would resolve them unless they happened to match on both properties, which is far less likely.

wrong.A: A longer run spreads the lane but cannot separate species that migrate identically, because the property being separated on is the same for both.
wrong.C: More SDS does not help: the problem is not incomplete denaturation but that mass is the only variable being measured.
wrong.D: A more sensitive dye reveals fainter bands, not bands hidden underneath one another at the same position.

questions.stem: A student measures the osmotic pressure of a 0.10 M solution of an unknown salt and wants to determine how many ions it releases per formula unit. The control that makes the measurement interpretable is:

choices.A: pure water measured in the same apparatus at the same temperature
choices.B: a 0.10 M glucose solution measured in the same apparatus
choices.C: a 0.20 M solution of the same unknown salt, measured identically
choices.D: a 0.10 M solution of a strong acid measured in the same apparatus

questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure depends on the total concentration of dissolved particles. Glucose does not dissociate, so a 0.10 M glucose solution gives the pressure expected from one particle per formula unit. The ratio of the salt's reading to that reference is the number of ions released. Without it the measurement is a number with nothing to compare against.

wrong.A: Pure water sets the instrument's zero but gives no scale, so it cannot distinguish a reading from two particles from one from three.
wrong.C: Doubling the concentration of the same unknown confirms the response is linear, but leaves the particle count per formula unit unknown.
wrong.D: A strong acid is itself an electrolyte of unknown particle count for this purpose, so it is not a reference for one particle per formula unit.

questions.stem: Which solution has the greatest buffer capacity at pH 7.4?

choices.A: 0.01 M acetic acid and 0.01 M sodium acetate, pKa 4.8
choices.B: 0.50 M acetic acid and 0.50 M sodium acetate, pKa 4.8
choices.C: 0.01 M dihydrogen phosphate and 0.01 M hydrogen phosphate, pKa 7.2
choices.D: 0.50 M dihydrogen phosphate and 0.50 M hydrogen phosphate, pKa 7.2

questions.explanation: Buffer capacity rises with concentration and is greatest when the pH is near the pKa. The phosphate pair has a pKa of 7.2, close to 7.4, and the concentrated pair has fifty times the material of the dilute one, so it resists added acid or base best on both counts.

wrong.A: This loses on both counts: a pKa two and a half units away and a low concentration.
wrong.B: Concentrated, but a pKa of 4.8 is far from 7.4, so the pair is almost entirely in its basic form and has little acid left to neutralise added base.
wrong.C: The right pKa but fifty times less material, so it is exhausted by a much smaller addition.

questions.stem: A reaction is thought to be first order in substrate. Which experiment would test that most directly?

choices.A: Measure the initial rate at several substrate concentrations and check whether rate is proportional to concentration
choices.B: Measure the rate at several temperatures and check whether it follows the Arrhenius equation
choices.C: Measure how long the reaction takes to go to completion at one concentration
choices.D: Measure the equilibrium constant at several concentrations

questions.explanation: Reaction order is defined by how rate depends on concentration, so varying concentration and watching the rate is the direct test. Initial rates are used because they avoid the complication of the concentration changing as the reaction proceeds.

wrong.B: Temperature dependence gives the activation energy. Reactions of every order obey the Arrhenius equation, so it says nothing about order.
wrong.C: A single concentration provides one data point, and order is a statement about how rate changes between concentrations.
wrong.D: An equilibrium constant describes the final position of the reaction, not the rate at which it gets there, and it does not vary with concentration.

questions.stem: Of the noble gases, xenon has the highest boiling point because:

choices.A: its larger electron cloud is more easily polarised, giving stronger dispersion forces
choices.C: it forms the strongest hydrogen bonds
choices.D: it has permanent dipoles that the lighter noble gases lack

questions.explanation: Dispersion forces arise from momentary fluctuations in an electron cloud, and a larger, more loosely held cloud distorts more readily. Xenon has the most electrons of the common noble gases, so its dispersion forces are strongest and it holds together to the highest temperature.

wrong.B: Noble gases are not meaningfully electronegative, and electronegativity decreases down a group in any case.
wrong.C: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen bound to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine. Noble gases have no hydrogen at all.
wrong.D: A single atom cannot have a permanent dipole; what it has are instantaneous, fluctuating ones.

questions.stem: Which atom has the largest first ionisation energy?

choices.D: Cl

questions.explanation: Ionisation energy rises across a period as nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, so the outermost electron is held more tightly. Chlorine is furthest to the right of these four and so holds its electrons most tightly.

wrong.A: Sodium has a single loosely held 3s electron and the lowest ionisation energy of the four.
wrong.B: Magnesium's filled 3s subshell gives it a local maximum relative to aluminium, but it is still far to the left of chlorine.
wrong.C: Aluminium's 3p electron is higher in energy and better shielded, so it is actually easier to remove than magnesium's.

questions.stem: A radiotracer has a half-life of 6.0 hours. What fraction of the original activity remains after 24 hours?
questions.explanation: Twenty-four hours is four half-lives, and each one halves the activity: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16. Counting half-lives rather than reaching for the exponential form is both faster and harder to get wrong.

wrong.A: 1/4 is two half-lives, which would be 12 hours.
wrong.B: 1/8 is three half-lives, which would be 18 hours. This is the commonest slip: counting the halvings but stopping one short.
wrong.D: 1/24 divides the time by the half-life and treats the result as a fraction, which confuses a count of half-lives with a fraction remaining.
